summary: On 25 January 2023 an engineer ran a command on a WAN router in Madrid to purge the IGP database. The command forced every router joined to the IGP to recompute topology, and Microsoft 365 and Azure were unreachable for many users for hours.

overview.background: Microsoft's WAN connects its data centers and the internet. Routers share routes using an interior gateway protocol (IGP), and BGP routers validate internet prefixes.
systems: Microsoft 365: Teams, SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Exchange Online
Microsoft Graph, Power BI, Intune, Defender
overview.impact: Many users could not reach Microsoft 365 services from 7:08 AM to about 12:43 PM UTC. SharePoint and OneDrive requests dropped about 10 percent against the prior week between 7:08 and 9:50 AM UTC.
overview.severity: A multi-service, multi-region event, concentrated in Asia Pacific and EMEA during business hours.
overview.gaps: The document gives no user counts.

diagrams.title: One command recomputes the whole network
diagrams.caption: The command ran across all IGP-joined routers on that vendor's platform. BGP routers then re-validated internet prefixes, which took about 1 hour 40 minutes to restore fully.

diagrams.caption: Microsoft planned to block commands with widespread impact, give real-time visibility of device activity and require SOP review. This picture shows the idea.

timeline.e: A planned WAN router change in Madrid triggers network-wide recomputation.
Monitoring alerts and DNS configurations are reviewed.
The incident is posted to the Service Health Dashboard.
Monitoring confirms the issue is in the WAN, not DNS.
The source is identified and automated recovery is already under way.
The WAN self-recovers and downstream services begin recovering.
The majority of services have recovered and the incident window ends.

rootCause.trigger: An engineer added WAN capacity in Madrid and ran a command to purge the IGP database.
rootCause.underlying: On one vendor's platform the command executes across all IGP-joined routers and forces topology recomputation. It was not on the authorization block list.
contributing: The SOP had been changed without re-testing or post-checks
Alerts fired within 5 minutes but the engineer was not told
The same operation ran on a second router 33 minutes later, creating a second wave

evidence.label: The process failure
evidence.body: Critically, our process was not followed as the change was not re-tested and did not include proper post-checks

evidence.label: The chain of events
evidence.body: This unqualified change led to a chain of events which culminated in the widespread impact of this incident.

evidence.label: A simulated command guard
evidence.body:
deny  clear igp database  (scope: all-routers)
require  change-ticket and second approver for  routing-protocol  commands
evidence.note: Shows an authorization rule. Syntax is invented and not any vendor's.

diagnose.step: Check whether the fault is DNS, WAN or application.
diagnose.why: Microsoft ruled out DNS by 7:40 AM.

diagnose.step: Look at recent network change activity.
diagnose.why: A Madrid router change matched the start.

diagnose.step: Check routing protocol state across routers.

correct.step: Let the network re-converge and watch recovery.
Stop a second run of the command.
correct.why: The same operation ran 33 minutes later.

correct.step: Move traffic off the affected path where possible.
correct.why: Moving SPO and ODB off Front Door did not help here.

verify.why: India packet loss was found later.

prevent.why: Microsoft noted the engineer was not informed.

fix.safety: Do not repeat a command on a second router until you have checked the first. A single mistake should not be run twice.

troubleshoot.scenario: An engineer ran a routine command on one router. Five minutes later alerts fire and many services are unreachable.
clues: The same task is due on another router
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
troubleshoot.answer: Pause the second run, confirm the fault is in the WAN, notify the engineer and incident manager, let recovery proceed and follow up with command blocking and tested procedures.

options: Purged the IGP database and forced recomputation on all joined routers

remediation.answer: Wide-impact commands need two approvals and a tested SOP.
Alerts must page the change owner as well as on-call.
Practise recovery from IGP recompute in a lab.

design.prompt: Design network operations so one command cannot affect all routers.
design.answer: Block risky commands by policy, require approvals, test procedures, add real-time visibility, and segment IGP domains.
